20:A mechanized audit hook (e.g. `claude_md_count_audit.py`, `cite_drift_audit.py`, `mcp_self_audit.py`; `sota_freshness_sweep.py` is FORWARD-REF/NOT-INSTALLED in this runtime) fires automatically on every relevant commit when installed, writes drift records to JSONL, and surfaces drift signals to disk. **The audit alone provides 0 protection** — only the audit-action-loop (audit fires → drift surfaces → bounded ship closes) protects against silent staleness.

117:4. **Atomic batch** — bundle related edits (root + MEMORY.md close entry) in a single `git add ... && git commit` invocation to minimize cross-session bundling risk. Specifically: parallel sessions can commit during the gap between `git add` and `git commit`, and bundle your staged edit into their unrelated commit. The single-invocation form prevents this race.
119:5. **Verify next audit fires `any_drift: false`** for the closed axis — if not, the fix didn't take. Codex postcommit review on the closing commit IS the verification gate.
123:Audit-failure is the worst defect class: a broken audit looks like it's working (entries appear in JSONL) while providing 0 protection. Worse: a working audit that surfaces drift but isn't actioned has the same effect — the mechanization runs, the data accumulates, but nothing closes the drift. Within 12-24h of accumulation, drift becomes "background noise" that humans/agents stop checking. The audit-action-loop is the consumer-side discipline that makes wired audits valuable.
128:- **Audit script itself is broken** — if JSONL records are empty (e.g. `{"ts":"..."}` only) or use wrong field names, fix the audit before closing drifts based on its output.
130:- **Cross-session ownership unclear** — if working tree shows uncommitted changes from a parallel session, prefer `git stash` + commit + restore over editing in-place; minimizes bundling risk.
134:- `.claude/rules/research-protocol.md` VERIFY corollary 2 (Audit producer-consumer coupling) — claude-sota-local invariant for this rule. Research-protocol's corollary 2 says "every state-correctness audit needs BOTH a write-side trigger wire AND a read-side consumer that surfaces regressions to a decision surface". This rule (`audit-action-loop.md`) IS the consumer-side closure discipline that satisfies that invariant.

8:tags: [context-management, compaction, overflow-recovery, token-estimation, transcript-validation, api-compaction]
13:Context overflow is a silent killer of agent reliability. When accumulated conversation history exceeds the model's context window:
15:- **API errors**: Requests fail with `context_length_exceeded` or similar errors
16:- **Manual intervention**: Operators must truncate transcripts, losing valuable context
17:- **Retry complexity**: Detecting overflow and retrying with compaction is error-prone
19:Agents need automatic compaction that preserves essential information while staying within token limits, with model-specific validation and reserve token floors to prevent immediate re-overflow.
23:Automatic session compaction triggered by context overflow errors, with smart reserve tokens and lane-aware retry. The system detects overflow, compacts the session transcript, validates the result, and retries the request—all transparently to the user.
27:- **Overflow detection**: Catches API errors indicating context length exceeded (`context_length_exceeded`, `prompt is too long`, etc.).
28:- **Auto-retry with compaction**: On overflow, the session is compacted and the request is retried automatically.
29:- **Reserve token floor**: Post-compaction, ensures a minimum number of tokens (default 20k) remain available to prevent immediate re-overflow.
30:- **Lane-aware compaction**: Uses hierarchical lane queuing (session → global) to prevent deadlocks during compaction.
31:- **Post-compaction verification**: Estimates token count after compaction and verifies it's less than the pre-compaction count.

305: - `STAGED` → `REJECTED-POST-PROBE`: axis-fail or Probe DAG REJECT

310: ### `@latest` resolution at execute time (per Wave 50 fire 8 Pattern A on Agent I F-4 — operationalizes CR-9 version-pin mandate)
311: 
312: Every install command in this manifest tagged `@latest` (e.g., `npm install -g @doobidoo/mcp-memory-service@latest`, `docker pull qdrant/qdrant:latest`, `npm install -g markdownlint-cli2@latest`) carries **implicit `@latest-acknowledged-D6-risk:2026-05-06` status** — the manifest planning intent is "pull newest at install execution per CR-6, with explicit D6 today-release-auto-upgrade risk acknowledgment per CR-9". At install execution, the operator MUST:
313: 
314: 1. Resolve the actual version (e.g., `npm view @doobidoo/mcp-memory-service version` returns `1.4.7` → install command becomes `npm install -g @doobidoo/mcp-memory-service@1.4.7`)
315: 2. Record both the `@latest` planning intent AND the resolved `@<resolved-version>` in `docs/install-provenance.md` under the install row (per CR-6 D6 risk-acknowledged contract)
316: 3. Pin the manifest install command to the resolved version post-install (manifest row updated from `@latest` to `@<resolved-version>` as part of `STAGED → INSTALLED` promotion)
317: 4. Re-evaluation trigger: per `docs/install-from-github-discipline.md §"When to re-install"` — the resolved-version pin holds until either a re-install is needed (per upstream changelog or sibling D6 evidence) OR the row's manifest age exceeds N-day re-evaluation cadence
318: 
319: **Rationale**: the manifest's `@latest` install commands ARE the SOTA-discipline contract per CR-6 fresh-from-github (do not pre-pin to stale versions in the planning document). The resolution-at-execute-time + provenance-recording gate satisfies CR-9 version-pin mandate without violating CR-6 fresh-from-github. The promotion-gate state machine above enforces this — a row cannot advance `STAGED → INSTALLED` until step 3 (resolved-version pin) lands in the manifest row.
320: 
321: **Scope**: applies to ALL install commands carrying raw `@latest` AND `@HEAD`-equivalent pulls (`git clone --depth 1 ... origin/main` without SHA pin). Does NOT apply to `@<version-tag>` pinned install commands (those satisfy CR-9 directly).

Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:34:Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:40:1. **Context Saving** — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:41:2. **Session Continuity** — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't `--continue`, previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:42:3. **Think in Code** — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and `console.log()`s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory paradigm across all 14 platforms: stop treating the LLM as a data processor, treat it as a code generator.

Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:866:Each `ctx_execute` call spawns an isolated subprocess with its own process boundary. Scripts can't access each other's memory or state. The subprocess runs your code, captures stdout, and only that stdout enters the conversation context. The raw data — log files, API responses, snapshots — never leaves the sandbox.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:878:When you call `ctx_search`, it returns relevant content snippets focused around matching query terms — not full documents, not approximations, the actual indexed content with smart extraction around what you're looking for. `ctx_fetch_and_index` extends this to URLs: fetch, convert HTML to markdown, chunk, index. The raw page never enters context. Use the `contentType` parameter to filter results by type (e.g. `code` or `prose`).
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:903:Indexed content persists in a per-project SQLite database at `~/.context-mode/content/`. When `ctx_fetch_and_index` is called for a URL that was already indexed within the last 24 hours, the fetch is skipped entirely. The model searches the existing index directly.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:910:This means `--continue` sessions preserve indexed docs across restarts. No re-fetching, no wasted context tokens.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:912:`ctx_stats` reports cache performance separately: hits, data avoided, network requests saved, and total context savings including cache.

Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:922:When the context window fills up, the agent compacts the conversation — dropping older messages to make room. Without session tracking, the model forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, what errors were resolved, and what you last asked for.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:924:Context Mode captures every meaningful event during your session and persists them in a per-project SQLite database. When the conversation compacts (or you resume with `--continue`, `--resume`, or `/resume`), your working state is rebuilt automatically — the model continues from your last prompt without asking you to repeat anything.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:926:> Resuming a non-latest session via `/resume <picker>` works the same way: the SessionStart hook detects the empty live-event table for the freshly issued session id and falls back to the most recent unconsumed snapshot for the project (`session_resume` table). The picker selects the conversation; context-mode rehydrates the prior working state.

Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:939:> **Note:** Full session continuity (capture + snapshot + restore) works on **Claude Code**, **Gemini CLI**, **VS Code Copilot**, **JetBrains Copilot**, **OpenCode**, and **KiloCode**. **OpenCode** and **KiloCode** use `experimental.chat.system.transform` as a SessionStart surrogate to inject the routing block and restore prior sessions, plus `chat.message` for user-prompt capture; full SessionStart hook support is not yet available ([#14808](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/14808), [#5409](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/5409)), but prior-session continuity and user-decision capture work fully. **Cursor** captures tool events via `preToolUse`/`postToolUse`, but `sessionStart` is currently rejected by Cursor's validator ([forum report](https://forum.cursor.com/t/unknown-hook-type-sessionstart/149566)), so session restore after compaction is not available yet. **OpenClaw** uses native gateway plugin hooks (`api.on()`) for full session continuity. **Pi Coding Agent** provides high session continuity via extension hooks (`tool_call`, `tool_result`, `session_start`, `session_before_compact`). **Codex CLI** provides partial hook-based session tracking through PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, and Stop; MCP tools work. **Antigravity**, **Kiro**, and **Zed** have no hook support in the current release, so session tracking is not available.

Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\docs\platform-support.md:175:When OpenCode triggers `experimental.session.compacting` (auto on context overflow OR manual `/compact`), context-mode saves a snapshot to its per-project SQLite store. Create a component that receives a nullable prop\n2. Access that prop's properties inside a closure (event handler)\n3. Add an early return guard: if (!prop) return null\n4. Pass null/undefined as the prop\n5. Component throws TypeError during render\n\n------------------------\n\n# React Compiler hoists closure property accesses into cache keys, causing TypeError\n\n## Summary\n\nThe React Compiler generates memoization cache keys by eagerly evaluating property accesses that were originally deferred inside closures (event handlers). This causes `TypeError` at render time when the object is `null`/`undefined`, even though the original code would never access the property during render.\n\nEarly returns (`if (!x) return null`) do not help — the compiler hoists the cache key check above the guard.\n\nJSX expressions are not affected — the compiler correctly extracts them to intermediate variables.\n\n## Reproduction\n\n[React Compiler Playground](https://playground.react.dev/)\n\n### Minimal case\n\n```jsx\nconst MyComponent = ({ user }) => {\n  const handleClick = () => {\n    console.log(user.name);\n  };\n\n  if (!user) return null;\n\n  return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click</button>;\n};\n```\n\nCompiled output:\n\n```js\nconst MyComponent = (t0) => {\n  const $ = _c(4);\n  const { user } = t0;\n\n  // Cache key runs BEFORE the null guard — throws when user is null\n  if ($[0] !== user.name) {\n    t1 = () => {\n      console.log(user.name);\n    };\n    $[0] = user.name;\n    $[1] = t1;\n  }\n\n  // The null guard comes AFTER — too late\n  if (!user) {\n    return null;\n  }\n\n  // ...\n};\n```\n\nThe source code is safe: `user.name` is only inside a click handler, and the early return prevents the button from rendering when `user` is null. But the compiler hoists `user.name` into a cache key that runs on **every render**, before the guard.\n\n### With nested access and JSX\n\n```jsx\nconst MyComponent = ({ user }) => {\n  const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);\n  const [link, setLink] = useState(null);\n\n  const handleClick = async () => {\n    console.log(user.company.id);\n    console.log(user.email);\n  };\n\n  return (\n    <div onClick={() => setVisible(false)}>\n      <span>{user?.email}</span>\n      <button onClick={handleClick}>Click</button>\n    </div>\n  );\n};\n```\n\nCompiled output (simplified):\n\n```js\n// The compiler hoists user.company.id and user.email from the closure\n// into cache key checks that run on EVERY render:\nif ($[0] !== user.company.id || $[1] !== user.email) {\n    t1 = async () => {\n      console.log(user.company.id);\n      console.log(user.email);\n    };\n    $[0] = user.company.id;\n    $[1] = user.email;\n    $[2] = t1;\n}\n\n// JSX — correctly extracted to variable (safe)\nconst t4 = user?.email;\nif ($[7] !== t4) {\n    t5 = <span>{t4}</span>;\n}\n```\n\n## Expected behavior\n\nThe compiler should not introduce runtime errors that the source code would not produce. Property accesses hoisted from closures into cache keys should be guarded, e.g. by extracting to intermediate variables:\n\n```js\nconst t0 = user?.name;\nif ($[0] !== t0) {\n    t1 = () => {\n      console.log(user.name);\n    };\n    $[0] = t0;\n    $[1] = t1;\n}\n```\n\n## Workarounds\n\n### 1. Extract to variables\n\nExtract property accesses into variables before using them in closures. The compiler then caches on the primitive values:\n\n```jsx\nconst companyId = user?.company?.id;\nconst email = user?.email;\n\nconst handleClick = async () => {\n  console.log(companyId);\n  console.log(email);\n};\n```\n\n### 2. Add optional chaining to every closure access\n\nAdding `?.` to every property access inside closures makes the compiler preserve it in cache keys. Note that **every** access must have `?.` — missing it on even one will produce an unsafe cache key for that property path:\n\n```jsx\nconst handleClick = async () => {\n  console.log(user?.company.id);\n  console.log(user?.email);\n};\n```\n\n### 3. Use nullish coalescing on destructuring\n\nUsing `?? {}` when destructuring the nullable object anywhere in the component signals to the compiler that the value can be nullish. This makes the compiler generate `?.` in **all** cache keys for that object:\n\n```jsx\nconst handleClick = () => {\n  const { name, email } = user ?? {};\n  console.log(name, email);\n};\n```\n\nThis produces `$[x] !== user?.name` instead of `$[x] !== user.name` in cache keys across the component.\n\n### 4. Add a null guard inside the closure\n\nAdding a null check before the property access inside the closure makes the compiler use the **object reference** as the cache key instead of the property path:\n\n```jsx\nconst handleClick = () => {\n  if (!user) return;\n  console.log(user.company.id);\n  console.log(user.email);\n};\n```\n\nThis produces `$[x] !== user` (the reference) instead of `$[x] !== user.company.id` (the property access) in the cache key. Comparing a reference to `null`/`undefined` never throws.\n\n## Environment\n\n- React Compiler (babel plugin via `react-compiler-runtime`)\n- Webpack 5 with HMR\n- Observed in both HMR hot-update bundles and regular builds\n\n\n### How often does this bug happen?\n\nEvery time\n\n### What version of React are you using?\n\n18.3.1\n\n### What version of React Compiler are you using?\n\n1.0.0","createdAt":"2026-02-11T13:34:24Z","labels":[{"id":"MDU6TGFiZWw0MDkyOTE1MQ==","name":"Type: Bug","description":"","color":"b60205"},{"id":"MDU6TGFiZWwxNTU5ODQxNjA=","name":"Status: Unconfirmed","description":"A potential issue that we haven't yet confirmed as a bug","color":"d4c5f9"}],"number":35762,"title":"[Compiler Bug]: Closure dependency cache keys eagerly evaluate property accesses, causing TypeError on nullable objects"},{"author":{"id":"U_kgDOBtEQIA","is_bot":false,"login":"rstar327","name":""},"body":"<!--\n  Please provide a clear and concise description of what the bug is. 972: #### Available MCP Tools
973: 
974: When running as an MCP server, Repomix provides the following tools:
975: 
976: 1. **pack_codebase**: Package a local code directory into a consolidated XML file for AI analysis
977:   - Parameters:
978:     - `directory`: Absolute path to the directory to pack
979:     - `compress`: (Optional, default: false) Enable Tree-sitter compression to extract essential code signatures and structure while removing implementation details. Reduces token usage by ~70% while preserving semantic meaning. Generally not needed since grep_repomix_output allows incremental content retrieval. Use only when you specifically need the entire codebase content for large repositories.
980:     - `includePatterns`: (Optional) Specify files to include using fast-glob patterns. Multiple patterns can be comma-separated (e.g., "**/*.{js,ts}", "src/**,docs/**"). Only matching files will be processed.
981:     - `ignorePatterns`: (Optional) Specify additional files to exclude using fast-glob patterns. Multiple patterns can be comma-separated (e.g., "test/**,*.spec.js", "node_modules/**,dist/**"). These patterns supplement .gitignore, .ignore, and built-in exclusions.
982:     - `topFilesLength`: (Optional, default: 10) Number of largest files by size to display in the metrics summary for codebase analysis.
983: 
984: 2. **attach_packed_output**: Attach an existing Repomix packed output file for AI analysis
985:   - Parameters:
986:     - `path`: Path to a directory containing repomix-output.xml or direct path to a packed repository XML file
987:     - `topFilesLength`: (Optional, default: 10) Number of largest files by size to display in the metrics summary
988:   - Features:
989:     - Accepts either a directory containing a repomix-output.xml file or a direct path to an XML file
990:     - Registers the file with the MCP server and returns the same structure as the pack_codebase tool
991:     - Provides secure access to existing packed outputs without requiring re-processing
992:     - Useful for working with previously generated packed repositories
993: 
994: 3. **pack_remote_repository**: Fetch, clone, and package a GitHub repository into a consolidated XML file for AI analysis
995:   - Parameters:
996:     - `remote`: GitHub repository URL or user/repo format (e.g., "yamadashy/repomix", "https://github.com/user/repo", or "https://github.com/user/repo/tree/branch")
997:     - `compress`: (Optional, default: false) Enable Tree-sitter compression to extract essential code signatures and structure while removing implementation details. Reduces token usage by ~70% while preserving semantic meaning. Generally not needed since grep_repomix_output allows incremental content retrieval. Use only when you specifically need the entire codebase content for large repositories.
998:     - `includePatterns`: (Optional) Specify files to include using fast-glob patterns. Multiple patterns can be comma-separated (e.g., "**/*.{js,ts}", "src/**,docs/**"). Only matching files will be processed.
999:     - `ignorePatterns`: (Optional) Specify additional files to exclude using fast-glob patterns. Multiple patterns can be comma-separated (e.g., "test/**,*.spec.js", "node_modules/**,dist/**"). These patterns supplement .gitignore, .ignore, and built-in exclusions.
1000:     - `topFilesLength`: (Optional, default: 10) Number of largest files by size to display in the metrics summary for codebase analysis.
1001: 
1002: 4. **read_repomix_output**: Read the contents of a Repomix-generated output file. Supports partial reading with line range specification for large files.
1003:   - Parameters:
1004:     - `outputId`: ID of the Repomix output file to read
1005:     - `startLine`: (Optional) Starting line number (1-based, inclusive). If not specified, reads from beginning.
1006:     - `endLine`: (Optional) Ending line number (1-based, inclusive). If not specified, reads to end.
1007:   - Features:
1008:     - Specifically designed for web-based environments or sandboxed applications
1009:     - Retrieves the content of previously generated outputs using their ID
1010:     - Provides secure access to packed codebase without requiring file system access
1011:     - Supports partial reading for large files
1012: 
1013: 5. **grep_repomix_output**: Search for patterns in a Repomix output file using grep-like functionality with JavaScript RegExp syntax
1014:   - Parameters:
1015:     - `outputId`: ID of the Repomix output file to search
1016:     - `pattern`: Search pattern (JavaScript RegExp regular expression syntax)
1017:     - `contextLines`: (Optional, default: 0) Number of context lines to show before and after each match. Overridden by beforeLines/afterLines if specified.
1018:     - `beforeLines`: (Optional) Number of context lines to show before each match (like grep -B). Takes precedence over contextLines.
1019:     - `afterLines`: (Optional) Number of context lines to show after each match (like grep -A). Takes precedence over contextLines.
1020:     - `ignoreCase`: (Optional, default: false) Perform case-insensitive matching
1021:   - Features:
1022:     - Uses JavaScript RegExp syntax for powerful pattern matching
1023:     - Supports context lines for better understanding of matches
1024:     - Allows separate control of before/after context lines
1025:     - Case-sensitive and case-insensitive search options
1026: 
1027: 6. **file_system_read_file**: Read a file from the local file system using an absolute path. Includes built-in security validation to detect and prevent access to files containing sensitive information.
1028:   - Parameters:
1029:     - `path`: Absolute path to the file to read
1030:   - Security features:
1031:     - Implements security validation using [Secretlint](https://github.com/secretlint/secretlint)
1032:     - Prevents access to files containing sensitive information (API keys, passwords, secrets)
1033:     - Validates absolute paths to prevent directory traversal attacks
1034: 
1035: 7. **file_system_read_directory**: List the contents of a directory using an absolute path. Returns a formatted list showing files and subdirectories with clear indicators.
1036:   - Parameters:
1037:     - `path`: Absolute path to the directory to list
1038:   - Features:
1039:     - Shows files and directories with clear indicators (`[FILE]` or `[DIR]`)
1040:     - Provides safe directory traversal with proper error handling
1041:     - Validates paths and ensures they are absolute
1042:     - Useful for exploring project structure and understanding codebase organization

1048: #### Installation
1049: 
1050: **1. Add the Repomix plugin marketplace:**
1051: 
1052: ```text
1053: /plugin marketplace add yamadashy/repomix
1054: ```
1055: 
1056: **2. Install plugins:**
1057: 
1058: ```text
1059: # Install MCP server plugin (recommended foundation)
1060: /plugin install repomix-mcp@repomix
1061: 
1062: # Install commands plugin (extends functionality)
1063: /plugin install repomix-commands@repomix
1064: 
1065: # Install repository explorer plugin (AI-powered analysis)
1066: /plugin install repomix-explorer@repomix
1067: ```
1068: 
1069: **Note**: The `repomix-mcp` plugin is recommended as a foundation. The `repomix-commands` plugin provides convenient slash commands, while `repomix-explorer` adds AI-powered analysis capabilities. While you can install them independently, using all three provides the most comprehensive experience.
1070: 
1071: **Alternatively, use the interactive plugin installer:**
1072: 
1073: ```text
1074: /plugin
1075: ```
1076: 
1077: This will open an interactive interface where you can browse and install available plugins.

33: The `suggest-compact.js` script runs on PreToolUse (Edit/Write) and:
34: 
35: 1. **Tracks tool calls** — Counts tool invocations in session
36: 2. **Threshold detection** — Suggests at configurable threshold (default: 50 calls)
37: 3. **Periodic reminders** — Reminds every 25 calls after threshold
38: 
39: ## Hook Setup
40: 
41: Add to your `~/.claude/settings.json`:
42: 
43: ```json
44: {
45:   "hooks": {
46:     "PreToolUse": [
47:       {
48:         "matcher": "Edit",
49:         "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "node ~/.claude/skills/strategic-compact/suggest-compact.js" }]
50:       },
51:       {
52:         "matcher": "Write",
53:         "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "node ~/.claude/skills/strategic-compact/suggest-compact.js" }]
54:       }
55:     ]
56:   }
57: }
58: ```
59: 
60: ## Configuration
61: 
62: Environment variables:
63: - `COMPACT_THRESHOLD` — Tool calls before first suggestion (default: 50)
64: 
65: ## Compaction Decision Guide
66: 
67: Use this table to decide when to compact:
68: 
69: | Phase Transition | Compact? | Why |
70: |-----------------|----------|-----|
71: | Research → Planning | Yes | Research context is bulky; plan is the distilled output |
72: | Planning → Implementation | Yes | Plan is in TodoWrite or a file; free up context for code |
73: | Implementation → Testing | Maybe | Keep if tests reference recent code; compact if switching focus |
74: | Debugging → Next feature | Yes | Debug traces pollute context for unrelated work |
75: | Mid-implementation | No | Losing variable names, file paths, and partial state is costly |
76: | After a failed approach | Yes | Clear the dead-end reasoning before trying a new approach |
77: 
78: ## What Survives Compaction
79: 
80: Understanding what persists helps you compact with confidence:
81: 
82: | Persists | Lost |
83: |----------|------|
84: | CLAUDE.md instructions | Intermediate reasoning and analysis |
85: | TodoWrite task list | File contents you previously read |
86: | Memory files (`~/.claude/memory/`) | Multi-step conversation context |
87: | Git state (commits, branches) | Tool call history and counts |
88: | Files on disk | Nuanced user preferences stated verbally |
89: 
90: ## Best Practices
91: 
92: 1. **Compact after planning** — Once plan is finalized in TodoWrite, compact to start fresh
93: 2. **Compact after debugging** — Clear error-resolution context before continuing
94: 3. **Don't compact mid-implementation** — Preserve context for related changes
95: 4. **Read the suggestion** — The hook tells you *when*, you decide *if*
96: 5. **Write before compacting** — Save important context to files or memory before compacting
97: 6. **Use `/compact` with a summary** — Add a custom message: `/compact Focus on implementing auth middleware next`
98: 
99: ## Token Optimization Patterns
100: 
101: ### Trigger-Table Lazy Loading

116:   return { didOverride: true, reserveTokens: minReserveTokens };
117: }

119: 
120: **API-based compaction (OpenAI Responses API):**
121: 
122: Some providers offer dedicated compaction endpoints that are more efficient than manual summarization:
123: 
124: ```typescript
125: // OpenAI's /responses/compact endpoint
126: const compacted = await responsesAPI.compact({
127:   messages: currentMessages,
128: });
129: 
130: // Returns a list of items that includes:
131: // - A special type=compaction item with encrypted_content
132: //   that preserves the model's latent understanding
133: // - Condensed conversation items
134: 
135: currentMessages = compacted.items;
136: ```
137: 
138: This approach has advantages:
139: - **Preserves latent understanding**: The `encrypted_content` maintains the model's compressed representation of the original conversation
140: - **More efficient**: Server-side compaction is faster than client-side summarization
141: - **Auto-compaction**: Can trigger automatically when `auto_compact_limit` is exceeded
142: 
143: **Two complementary approaches:**
144: 
145: This pattern describes **reactive compaction** (detect overflow, compact, retry). An alternative approach is **preventive filtering** (reduce context at ingestion), used by systems like HyperAgent for browser accessibility tree extraction. Preventive filtering can delay or eliminate the need for reactive compaction by keeping context leaner from the start.
146:

2: title: Context-Minimization Pattern
3: status: emerging
4: authors: ["Nikola Balic (@nibzard)"]
5: based_on: ["Luca Beurer-Kellner et al. (2025)"]
6: category: Context & Memory
7: source: "https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08837"
8: tags: [context-hygiene, taint-removal, prompt-injection]
9: ---
10: 
11: ## Problem
12: 
13: In long agent sessions, raw user text and tool outputs often remain in-context long after they are needed. If those tokens include adversarial instructions, they can silently bias later reasoning steps, even when the current step is unrelated. This creates delayed prompt-injection risk and unnecessary context bloat.
14: 
15: ## Solution
16: 
17: **Purge or redact** untrusted segments once they've served their purpose:
18: 
19: - After transforming input into a safe intermediate (query, structured object), strip the original prompt from context.
20: - Subsequent reasoning sees **only trusted data**, eliminating latent injections.
21: - A **strong variant** also removes intermediate LLM outputs that may have been tainted.
22: 
23: Treat context as a staged pipeline: ingest untrusted text, transform it, then aggressively discard the original tainted material. Keep only signed-off structured artifacts that downstream steps are allowed to consume.
24: 
25: ```pseudo
26: sql = LLM("to SQL", user_prompt)
27: remove(user_prompt)              # tainted tokens gone
28: rows = db.query(sql)
29: answer = LLM("summarize rows", rows)
30: ```
31: 
32: ## Example
33: 
34: ```mermaid
35: flowchart LR
36:     A[User Prompt] --> B[Extract Intent]
37:     B --> C[Remove Original]
38:     C --> D[Trusted Data]
39:     D --> E[Execute Safely]
40:     A -.removed.-> C
41: ```
42: 
43: ## How to use it
44: 
45: Customer-service chat, medical Q&A, database query generation, any multi-turn flow where initial text shouldn't steer later steps.
46: 
47: ## Trade-offs
48: 
49: * **Pros:** Simple; no extra models needed; helps prevent [context window anxiety](context-window-anxiety-management.md) by reducing overall context usage; provides compliance benefits (HIPAA/GDPR data minimization).
50: * **Cons:** Later turns lose conversational nuance; may hurt UX; overly aggressive minimization can remove useful context; risks broken referential coherence when earlier turns are referenced ("the function I mentioned before").
51: 
52: ## References
53: 
54: * Beurer-Kellner et al., §3.1 (6) Context-Minimization.
55: * [Building Companies with Claude Code](https://claude.com/blog/building-companies-with-claude-code) - Emphasizes discrete phase separation and distilled handoffs to prevent context contamination.
56: * OpenAI, [Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop](https://openai.com/index/unrolling-the-codex-agent-loop/) - Documents context auto-compaction in production.

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /**
3:  * Strategic Compact Suggester
4:  *
5:  * Cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux)
6:  *
7:  * Runs on PreToolUse or periodically to suggest manual compaction at logical intervals
8:  *
9:  * Why manual over auto-compact:
10:  * - Auto-compact happens at arbitrary points, often mid-task
11:  * - Strategic compacting preserves context through logical phases
12:  * - Compact after exploration, before execution
13:  * - Compact after completing a milestone, before starting next
14:  */
15: 
16: const fs = require('fs');
17: const path = require('path');
18: const {
19:   getTempDir,
20:   writeFile,
21:   log
22: } = require('../lib/utils');
23: 
24: async function main() {
25:   // Track tool call count (increment in a temp file)
26:   // Use a session-specific counter file based on session ID from environment
27:   // or parent PID as fallback
28:   const sessionId = (process.env.CLAUDE_SESSION_ID || 'default').replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9_-]/g, '') || 'default';
29:   const counterFile = path.join(getTempDir(), `claude-tool-count-${sessionId}`);
30:   const rawThreshold = parseInt(process.env.COMPACT_THRESHOLD || '50', 10);
31:   const threshold = Number.isFinite(rawThreshold) && rawThreshold > 0 && rawThreshold <= 10000
32:     ? rawThreshold
33:     : 50;
34: 
35:   let count = 1;
36: 
37:   // Read existing count or start at 1
38:   // Use fd-based read+write to reduce (but not eliminate) race window
39:   // between concurrent hook invocations
40:   try {
41:     const fd = fs.openSync(counterFile, 'a+');
42:     try {
43:       const buf = Buffer.alloc(64);
44:       const bytesRead = fs.readSync(fd, buf, 0, 64, 0);
45:       if (bytesRead > 0) {
46:         const parsed = parseInt(buf.toString('utf8', 0, bytesRead).trim(), 10);
47:         // Clamp to reasonable range — corrupted files could contain huge values
48:         // that pass Number.isFinite() (e.g., parseInt('9'.repeat(30)) => 1e+29)
49:         count = (Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed > 0 && parsed <= 1000000)
50:           ? parsed + 1
51:           : 1;
52:       }
53:       // Truncate and write new value
54:       fs.ftruncateSync(fd, 0);
55:       fs.writeSync(fd, String(count), 0);
56:     } finally {
57:       fs.closeSync(fd);
58:     }
59:   } catch {
60:     // Fallback: just use writeFile if fd operations fail
61:     writeFile(counterFile, String(count));
62:   }
63: 
64:   // Suggest compact after threshold tool calls
65:   if (count === threshold) {
66:     log(`[StrategicCompact] ${threshold} tool calls reached - consider /compact if transitioning phases`);
67:   }
68: 
69:   // Suggest at regular intervals after threshold (every 25 calls from threshold)
70:   if (count > threshold && (count - threshold) % 25 === 0) {
71:     log(`[StrategicCompact] ${count} tool calls - good checkpoint for /compact if context is stale`);
72:   }
73: 
74:   process.exit(0);
75: }
76: 
77: main().catch(err => {
78:   console.error('[StrategicCompact] Error:', err.message);
79:   process.exit(0);
80: });

159:## 12. Rewind-first over correct-layered (Thariq 2026-04-16)
163:When an approach fails, **rewind** (double-Esc or `/rewind`) to the last sound state and re-prompt with what you learned — don't layer corrections on broken context.
166:- **Correcting** keeps the failed attempt + correction message + fix in context:
167:  `reads + 2 failed attempts + 2 corrections + fix` ← context rot accelerator
168:- **Rewinding** cuts the failed tail, keeps the good reads, re-prompts once:
171:### When to rewind vs. each alternative
174:| Claude explored five files, tried approach A, it failed | **Rewind** to after the reads, re-prompt "don't use A, foo doesn't expose that — go straight to B" | Keep the expensive reads, drop the failed attempt |
180:When rewinding, optionally ask Claude to summarize its learnings first — a message to the previous iteration from its future self: *"I tried X and it didn't work because Y; approach Z is the move."* Carries the lesson, drops the wreckage.
185:`CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=80` → autocompact fires at ~800k. Rely on the layered strategy:
187:2. **Rewind** on failures — keep reads, drop failed tail

77: ## Rewinding Instead of Correcting
78: 
79: If Thariq had to pick one habit that signals good context management, it's **rewind**.
80: 
81: In Claude Code, double-tapping Esc (or running `/rewind`) lets you jump back to any previous message and re-prompt from there. The messages after that point are dropped from the context.
82: 
83: **Correcting** (saying "no, try B" after a failed attempt A) leaves the failed attempt in context:
84: > context = reads + 2 failed attempts + 2 corrections + the fix
85: 
86: **Rewinding** (going back to before the failed attempt and re-prompting with what you learned) is cleaner:
87: > context = reads + one informed prompt + the fix
88: 
89: Rewind is often the better approach. For example, Claude reads five files, tries an approach, and it doesn't work. Your instinct may be to type "that didn't work, try X instead." But the better move is to rewind to just after the file reads, and re-prompt with what you learned: "Don't use approach A, the foo module doesn't expose that — go straight to B."
90: 
91: You can also use **"summarize from here"** to have Claude summarize its learnings and create a handoff message, kind of like a message to the previous iteration of Claude from its future self that tried something and it didn't work.
92: 
93: <img src="assets/thariq-26-4-16/9.png" alt="Correcting vs rewinding diagram" width="50%" />
94: 
95: <img src="assets/thariq-26-4-16/10.png" alt="Rewind with summarize from here" width="50%" />

159: ## 12. Rewind-first over correct-layered (Thariq 2026-04-16)
160: 
161: Reference: Z:/repos/deps/claude-code-best-practice-shan/tips/claude-thariq-tips-16-apr-26.md:79-95
162: 
163: When an approach fails, **rewind** (double-Esc or `/rewind`) to the last sound state and re-prompt with what you learned — don't layer corrections on broken context.
164: 
165: ### Why
166: - **Correcting** keeps the failed attempt + correction message + fix in context:
167:   `reads + 2 failed attempts + 2 corrections + fix` ← context rot accelerator
168: - **Rewinding** cuts the failed tail, keeps the good reads, re-prompts once:
169:   `reads + one informed prompt + fix` ← cleaner, cheaper
170: 
171: ### When to rewind vs. each alternative
172: | Situation | Use | Why |
173: |---|---|---|
174: | Claude explored five files, tried approach A, it failed | **Rewind** to after the reads, re-prompt "don't use A, foo doesn't expose that — go straight to B" | Keep the expensive reads, drop the failed attempt |
175: | Mid-task but session bloated with stale debugging | `/compact <hint>` | Steer the lossy summary: `/compact focus on auth refactor, drop test debugging` |
176: | Genuinely new task, one fact found in 100k of exploration | `/clear` + you-written brief | Zero rot, you control what carries |
177: | Next step = lots of output, only conclusion matters | Subagent | Intermediate tool noise GC'd on child exit |
178: 
179: ### "Summarize from here" handoff
180: When rewinding, optionally ask Claude to summarize its learnings first — a message to the previous iteration from its future self: *"I tried X and it didn't work because Y; approach Z is the move."* Carries the lesson, drops the wreckage.
181: 
182: ### Autocompact is a safety net, not the primary tool
183: Thariq `:123-125`: "the model is at its least intelligent point when compacting" — autocompact fires **without a steering hint** and usually mid-rot. For complex automation with SOTA references, autocompact is the *last resort*.
184: 
185: `CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=80` → autocompact fires at ~800k. Rely on the layered strategy:
186: 1. **Proactive `/compact <hint>`** at ~300k — steered summary before rot
187: 2. **Rewind** on failures — keep reads, drop failed tail

Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:34:Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides.
Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:41:2. **Session Continuity** — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't `--continue`, previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate.

Z:/repos/deps/context-mode\README.md:939:> **Note:** Full session continuity (capture + snapshot + restore) works on **Claude Code**, **Gemini CLI**, **VS Code Copilot**, **JetBrains Copilot**, **OpenCode**, and **KiloCode**. **OpenCode** and **KiloCode** use `experimental.chat.system.transform` as a SessionStart surrogate to inject the routing block and restore prior sessions, plus `chat.message` for user-prompt capture; full SessionStart hook support is not yet available ([#14808](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/14808), [#5409](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/5409)), but prior-session continuity and user-decision capture work fully. **Cursor** captures tool events via `preToolUse`/`postToolUse`, but `sessionStart` is currently rejected by Cursor's validator ([forum report](https://forum.cursor.com/t/unknown-hook-type-sessionstart/149566)), so session restore after compaction is not available yet. **OpenClaw** uses native gateway plugin hooks (`api.on()`) for full session continuity. **Pi Coding Agent** provides high session continuity via extension hooks (`tool_call`, `tool_result`, `session_start`, `session_before_compact`). **Codex CLI** provides partial hook-based session tracking through PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, and Stop; MCP tools work. **Antigravity**, **Kiro**, and **Zed** have no hook support in the current release, so session tracking is not available.

All tool lifecycle hooks (`after_tool_call`, `before_compaction`, `session_start`) fire via the native gateway plugin. User decisions aren't captured but file edits, git ops, errors, and tasks are fully tracked. Falls back to DB snapshot reconstruction if compaction hooks fail on older gateway versions. .claude/plugins/cache/context-mode/context-mode/1.0.111\README.md:34:Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides.
.claude/plugins/cache/context-mode/context-mode/1.0.111\README.md:41:2. **Session Continuity** — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't `--continue`, previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate.

.claude/plugins/cache/context-mode/context-mode/1.0.111\README.md:939:> **Note:** Full session continuity (capture + snapshot + restore) works on **Claude Code**, **Gemini CLI**, **VS Code Copilot**, **JetBrains Copilot**, **OpenCode**, and **KiloCode**. **OpenCode** and **KiloCode** use `experimental.chat.system.transform` as a SessionStart surrogate to inject the routing block and restore prior sessions, plus `chat.message` for user-prompt capture; full SessionStart hook support is not yet available ([#14808](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/14808), [#5409](https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/5409)), but prior-session continuity and user-decision capture work fully. **Cursor** captures tool events via `preToolUse`/`postToolUse`, but `sessionStart` is currently rejected by Cursor's validator ([forum report](https://forum.cursor.com/t/unknown-hook-type-sessionstart/149566)), so session restore after compaction is not available yet. **OpenClaw** uses native gateway plugin hooks (`api.on()`) for full session continuity. **Pi Coding Agent** provides high session continuity via extension hooks (`tool_call`, `tool_result`, `session_start`, `session_before_compact`). **Codex CLI** provides partial hook-based session tracking through PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, and Stop; MCP tools work. **Antigravity**, **Kiro**, and **Zed** have no hook support in the current release, so session tracking is not available.
